description: Team Mission Atlas is building the Moon→Mars Mission Trainer, an interactive app where students operate lunar or Martian outposts and make engineering trade-offs. Our prototype uses official NASA Moon-to-Mars architecture data. We welcome teammates interested in software, game design, AI/ML, data visualization, UI/UX, and space exploration.
summary:
Can you keep a Moon base alive until sunrise?

Gaia Lunar Systems: The First Night is an interactive browser-based mission trainer that introduces children ages 7–12 to the challenges of lunar exploration.

Players select two crew specialists and navigate six mission decisions while managing oxygen, water, power, spare parts, crew health, and habitat safety. Every choice involves trade-offs, and unexpected events test their planning and problem-solving skills.

The game connects real NASA science with an engaging fictional mission. NASA's DONKI space-weather data provides solar-flare observations, while NASA's Moon-to-Mars Architecture-Driven Technology Gaps introduce engineering challenges involving lunar dust, power, water systems, electronics, and exploration.

Our central lesson: good decisions do not always guarantee good outcomes.

Mission Control reviews each decision separately from whether the mission survived, helping children understand uncertainty, risk, and engineering judgment. Gameplay probabilities and scoring are simplified educational models, not NASA mission predictions.

Built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, the game features interactive resources, NASA references, science facts, and replayable missions.

Our goal is to inspire young explorers by turning space science into decisions they can experience and learn from.
details:
Gaia Lunar Systems: The First Night

Can a young astronaut make the decisions needed to survive a lunar night?

Gaia Lunar Systems: The First Night is an interactive educational mission simulator created for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, addressing the Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge.

How the game works

The player becomes the leader of a fictional lunar outpost and selects two specialists from four available roles: Medical Officer, Engineer, Field Specialist, and Scientist.

Across six mission turns, the player manages six essential resources: crew health, habitat integrity, spare parts, electrical power, water, and oxygen.

Every decision creates a trade-off. Players may take a calculated risk, choose a safer response, or invest resources for future benefits. Some decisions produce uncertain outcomes, demonstrating why planning and managing risk matter in exploration.

The mission takes place across a simplified 30-day period, progressing from sunlight into the challenging lunar night.

NASA science and data integration

We integrate two primary NASA resources:

NASA DONKI (Space Weather Database): Provides real solar-flare observations used as scientific context for the game's solar-event scenario. The application can retrieve recent DONKI observations and retains a sourced historical event as a fallback.

NASA Moon-to-Mars Architecture-Driven Technology Gaps: Provides real engineering challenge references related to lunar dust, electrical power, water systems, extreme-environment electronics, equipment maintenance, and surface mobility.

Players can explore short science facts and follow source links to learn more.

NASA observations are clearly distinguished from the game's fictional events. Resource values, probabilities, mission consequences, and decision scores are simplified educational models, not validated NASA engineering predictions.

What makes our approach creative?

Instead of simply presenting information about the Moon, the game invites children to make decisions involving competing needs.

At the end of each mission, Mission Control reviews the player's individual choices using Good, OK, and Poor ratings, with accessible explanations.

Importantly, decision ratings are separated from mission survival. This illustrates a central principle of decision-making under uncertainty: a reasonable decision can have an unfortunate outcome, and an unwise decision can sometimes succeed.

The current scoring rubric is simplified and provisional; it should not be interpreted as an objective measure of optimal astronaut decisions.

Technology and implementation

The application uses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with a separate JavaScript game engine.

It includes responsive gameplay, resource tracking, specialist selection, deterministic test scenarios, replayable events, accessible decision explanations, and a read-only serverless interface for NASA space-weather data.

The source code is publicly available on GitHub, and the playable application is hosted on Vercel.

Development and testing

Our team combined game-system design, software development, scientific-source review, and youth-centered usability feedback.

Automated tests and multiple manual game sessions helped identify and correct interface and game-logic issues. Informal youth feedback informed improvements to the readability of choices and the Mission Control explanations.

These activities demonstrate iterative prototype development, not formal evidence of educational effectiveness.

Intended impact

Our goal is to make space exploration engaging and understandable for children ages 7–12 while introducing them to resource management, uncertainty, scientific evidence, and engineering judgment.

We want children not only to learn what astronauts face, but to discover how engineers think.

Project website: https://gaia-lunar-systems-2026.vercel.app

Source code: https://github.com/oluwafemidiakhoa/gaia-lunar-systems-2026
